source_read: PDF PDFs/MDMA/Bedi_2009_MDMASociabilityNeuralResponse.pdf: Bedi et al. (2009), Psychopharmacology 207:73-83, the published article (11 pages; PDF page 1 = p. 73). Text by pdftotext -layout; every page looked at on the rendered page at 150 dpi; Tables 1 to 4 and Figures 1 to 4 at 300 dpi; Figure 2 and the bar charts of Figures 3 and 4 also measured in the embedded images (calibrated on the axis ticks).

results.corrected_extracted: 9 healthy volunteers with earlier ecstasy use (7 men, 2 women; 2 to 300 occasions), double blind, MDMA 0.75 and 1.5 mg/kg in ascending order and placebo placed at random among the sessions. In the scanner they saw blocks of happy, neutral, angry, fearful, disgusted and sad faces and rated each expression as unpleasant, neutral or pleasant with a button box. Accuracy of these ratings, as marginal means across all the facial expressions (standard error), was 0.89 (0.04), 0.91 (0.01) and 0.86 (0.02) on placebo, 0.75 and 1.5 mg/kg (F(2,16) 0.9); reaction time was 1,345.7 (45.6), 1,168.9 (79.5) and 1,292.3 (115.5), the unit printed as microseconds (F(2,16) 3.1). Neither test is marked significant, nor is the drug-by-emotion-type interaction for accuracy (F(10,80) 1.2) or reaction time (F(10,80) 0.6); the text says MDMA did not affect the accuracy of emotion recognition or reaction time. Editors' calculation: degrees of freedom of 10 and 80 fit six kinds of faces in 9 people, so the disgusted and sad faces, which the Methods say were not used in the analyses, appear to be included in these means; F(2,16) 3.1 gives p of about .07.
results.corrected_locator: Materials and methods > Participants; Protocol, 1st and 4th paragraphs (pp. 74-75); Results, 1st and 5th paragraphs and Table 1 (p. 77); Table 3, the four emotion-recognition (ER) rows with notes c and d (p. 78)
results.note: Numbers confirmed at rendered p. 78 (Table 3 in the journal). Means cover all facial expressions (df fit six face types); responses were unpleasant/neutral/pleasant ratings, not named emotions. This paper states 20-second blocks, no per-face time.
results.suggested_source_read: PDF PDFs/MDMA/Bedi_2009_MDMASociabilityNeuralResponse.pdf (published article, pp. 73-83; all pages read on the rendered page at 150 dpi, Tables 1 to 4 and Figures 1 to 4 at 300 dpi)
results.claim_wording: For the editor: the claim's 'no change in the accuracy or speed of recognising them' rests on non-significant differences in a three-way rating (unpleasant, neutral, pleasant); 'no significant change' is what Table 3 shows.

format_note: Card items: each index has two entries. The first is the content verdict (confirmed, or corrected with the whole corrected text and a 'reason'). The second is a wrong-location entry that only moves the page and locator from 'PMC HTML' (the author manuscript the first reader read) to the journal pages of the published PDF; nothing was found at a wrong place in the manuscript layout. scripts/editor/adj_r2.py applies both entries.

page: pp. 77-78; locator: Results, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (p. 77); Table 3 and Figure 2 with its legend (p. 78)

Imaging: left amygdala response to angry against neutral faces was lower at 1.5 mg/kg than on placebo (uncorrected p < .005; corrected p = .052) and not changed for fearful faces; right ventral striatum response to happy against neutral faces was higher at 0.75 mg/kg than on placebo (corrected p < .05) and at 1.5 mg/kg did not survive correction; activity in visual and motor cortex during the motor-visual task fell at 1.5 mg/kg (uncorrected p < .005). In the scanner volunteers rated each face as unpleasant, neutral or pleasant; the accuracy and the speed of these ratings did not change significantly (accuracy 0.89, 0.91 and 0.86 on placebo, 0.75 and 1.5 mg/kg, F(2,16) 0.9; reaction time F(2,16) 3.1).
key_findings.reason: The imaging statements are confirmed (the paper says right ventral striatum). Only the last clause changes: Table 3 shows non-significant differences (reaction-time means 1,345.7, 1,168.9 and 1,292.3; F(2,16) 3.1, p of about .07 by the editors' calculation), not an absence of change, and the task was a three-way rating, not naming emotions (p. 75). The paper's own sentence is unhedged ('did not affect').

page: pp. 81-82; locator: Discussion, 8th to 11th paragraphs

The Introduction says increased sociability and decreased defensiveness are cited by people who use ecstasy as a motivator to use it (citing Sumnall et al. 2006) and that human laboratory studies of 1 to 2 mg/kg report increased extroversion, friendliness, sociability, talkativeness and closeness, with some studies not finding them; this paper's data do not address why people take MDMA.
key_findings.reason: Only 'a survey' is removed: this paper cites Sumnall et al. (2006) without describing its design, and the card says that paper was not read. Everything else is confirmed.

reporting_issues.correction: issue: The abstract says 1.5 mg/kg increased self-reported sociability compared with placebo. Table 3 gives placebo against 1.5 mg/kg as t(8) 2.5, p = .04, and the text and Figure 2 legend call it a marginal difference, against the paper's own post hoc alpha of .01.
reporting_issues.reason: Content confirmed; the effects table is Table 3 in the published article (Table 2 in the manuscript).

issue: The 'feel drug' values in Table 3 are printed as standard deviations (5.0, 4.6, 4.0) but behave like standard errors: t(8) 16.1 for 1.5 mg/kg against placebo implies an SD of the paired difference of about 14, more than standard deviations of 5.0 and 4.0 could give (at most 9.0) (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.reason: Confirmed and recomputed (77.3 x 3 / 16.1 = 14.4; the other two contrasts give 18.0 and 17.1). Changes: Table 3 in the published article, and the bound that makes the point certain (an SD of a difference cannot exceed the sum of the two SDs).

page: pp. 74, 81-82; locator: Materials and methods > Protocol, 1st paragraph (p. 74); Discussion, 10th paragraph (pp. 81-82)

risk_of_bias.note: Agree with the design (human-laboratory, within-person, order only partly randomised), the instrument (RoB 2 with the crossover domain and the editors' dose-comparison domain) and the overall judgment of high. Two remarks that do not change it: for the self-rated 'sociable' item the measurement domain could be argued up to high (all volunteers knew ecstasy, the 1.5 mg/kg dose was plainly felt, the blind was not checked); and the imaging tests on extracted signal reuse the peak voxels chosen by the same contrasts, so they add no independent support.

interpretation_gap.note: Agree with substantial. The abstract gives the sociability difference from placebo and the amygdala result without the paper's own qualifiers (marginal, p = .04 against a post hoc alpha of .01; corrected p = .052), and its conclusion offers a mechanism the study did not test; the Discussion itself notes that the striatum response rose at the dose at which 'sociable' ratings did not (p. 80).

missed: Emotion-recognition task and its numbers (Materials and methods > Protocol, 4th paragraph, p. 75; Results, 5th paragraph, p. 77; Table 3, p. 78): volunteers rated each stimulus as unpleasant, neutral or pleasant with a button box, so 'accuracy' is the accuracy of a three-way rating, not of naming an emotion. Six kinds of faces (happy, neutral, angry, fearful, disgusted, sad) and radios were shown in 20-second blocks, four runs a session (Fig. 1, p. 76); the card's design_detail names four kinds, and the paper does not say how long each face stayed on screen. Table 3 gives marginal means across all facial expressions with standard errors: accuracy 0.89 (0.04), 0.91 (0.01), 0.86 (0.02), F(2,16) 0.9; reaction time 1,345.7 (45.6), 1,168.9 (79.5), 1,292.3 (115.5), unit printed as microseconds, F(2,16) 3.1; drug by emotion type F(10,80) 1.2 and 0.6; none is marked significant. Editors' calculation: degrees of freedom (10,80) fit six kinds of faces, although the Methods say the disgusted and sad blocks were not used in the analyses; F(2,16) 3.1 gives p of about .07 and a partial eta-squared of 0.28. The paper calls 0.28 very large for the sociability interaction and says an effect above .23 may have missed significance because of the sample size (Friendliness), yet states that MDMA did not affect reaction time.

Tests on extracted signal, not in the card (Results, 6th and 7th paragraphs, pp. 77-78; Figures 3 and 4, p. 79): signal from 10-mm spheres around the peak voxels gave, for the left amygdala, F(2,16) 7.24, p < .01, lower at 1.5 mg/kg than on placebo (t(8) 3.34, p < .05) and than at 0.75 mg/kg (t(8) 2.44, p < .05); for the ventral striatum, F(2,16) 8.41, p < .005, higher than placebo at both doses (0.75 mg/kg t(8) 5.51, p < .005; 1.5 mg/kg t(8) 2.44, p < .05). The spheres were centred on peaks found with the same contrasts in the same data, so these tests are not independent of the voxel tests (reader's comment). Reader's measurement of the bars in the embedded images (arbitrary units; placebo, 0.75, 1.5 mg/kg): amygdala, angry minus neutral faces, about +0.12, +0.02, -0.27; ventral striatum, happy minus neutral faces, about -0.12, +0.20, +0.11. Each value is a difference from neutral faces, so a change in the response to neutral faces would give the same picture (reader's comment).

Table 4 (p. 80), not used in the card: at p < .001 uncorrected (clusters of at least 80 mm3) the main effect of drug on the angry-against-neutral contrast appears in 20 clusters outside the a priori regions (Z 3.35 to 4.33; 88 to 848 mm3; frontal, parietal, temporal, motor and cingulate cortex, caudate, putamen, insula, cerebellum), against Z 2.91 and 80 mm3 (10 voxels) for the amygdala cluster at its own threshold of p < .005. There is one such cluster for fearful faces, one besides the ventral striatum (Z 2.93, 240 mm3) for happy faces and four for the motor-visual task. Reader's comment: the drug effect on the angry-faces contrast was not specific to the amygdala; the table gives no direction for these effects.

The authors themselves note (Discussion, 4th paragraph, p. 80) that at 0.75 mg/kg the brain response to happy faces rose without any change in 'sociable' ratings; this sits badly with the abstract's conclusion that MDMA may raise sociability by enhancing responses to reward, and belongs in cannot_establish.

Second-hand, from the limitations (Discussion, 8th paragraph, p. 81): the authors cite an earlier PET study (Gamma et al. 2000, not read) in which MDMA lowered blood flow in the left amygdala independent of task, and say confounding effects of MDMA on brain blood vessels cannot be ruled out; this bears directly on the amygdala result.

Timing and setting (Materials and methods > Protocol, 2nd and 4th paragraphs, p. 75): volunteers were taken to the imaging centre about 45 minutes after the capsule; imaging began 80.8 (±6.6) minutes after it on placebo, 82.1 (±12.6) at 0.75 mg/kg and 91.4 (±10.5) at 1.5 mg/kg, about 10 minutes later in the 1.5 mg/kg sessions. The paper does not say whether volunteers were alone or with other people when they rated 'sociable'.

Not stated in the paper: the length of the visual analogue scales (only their end labels are given, p. 75), so '92 of 100' in the card's assessor_blinding field is an assumption (Table 3 gives 91.8 as the mean peak change from baseline); and whether '±7.15' for the days between sessions is an SD (p. 82; design_detail says SD 7.2). The Results text describes the corrected amygdala result as 'significant at p=0.052' (p. 77), which could be added to reporting issue 1.

Figure 2 (p. 78), reader's measurement in the embedded image, calibrated on the axis ticks (the 135-minute points reproduce Table 3: -6.3, -9.5, 19.7): mean change in the 'sociable' rating on placebo, 0.75 and 1.5 mg/kg was about -4, -6.5 and -4 at 30 minutes; -3, -7 and +12 at 60; -4, -20 and +2 at 210; -3, -10 and -1.5 at 240. The 0.75 mg/kg rating was below placebo at every time and lowest at 210 minutes (standard error about 6); only the 135-minute contrasts are printed. Friendliness change at 1.5 mg/kg was about +0.74 at 60 minutes (standard error about 0.4) and +0.24 at 240 minutes; placebo and 0.75 mg/kg stayed between about -0.07 and 0. The units of the Friendliness score are not stated.

Numbering in the published article: Table 1 (ecstasy use and recent drug use) and Table 2 (lifetime use of other drugs) are on p. 77, the effects table is Table 3 on p. 78 (called Table 2 in the card's effect_sizes and multiplicity_correction fields) and the brain table is Table 4 on p. 80. Table 2 also shows that 8 of the 9 had used opiates and 5 tranquillizers at least once. The card's verification.source_read can now name the PDF.
